content: 1. At the start of the guideline development meetings, each member of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) was required to present their declaration of interests. Members of the GDG and evidence teams attending the meetings were asked to provide updates if there were any changes to their declarations of interests. If changes occurred, the WHO Steering Group reviewed and managed these updates according to established protocols. 2. All participants, including the GDG, Evidence Review Group (ERG), evidence teams, and meeting observers, were required to sign a confidentiality agreement. Staff from the International Labour Organization (ILO) were subject to declarations of interest and conflict of interest management in accordance with ILO policies, such as the Office Directive on Ethics in the Office (143). Similarly, WHO staff were subject to the WHO Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct (144) and the Standards of Conduct for the International Civil Service. 3. Meeting observers and representatives of organizations were not required to complete declarations of interest because they did not actively participate in the discussions related to guideline development. All contributors declared no conflicts of interest, except for those explicitly listed. 4. A summary of declared interests and their management is provided in Annex 2. For example: Capucine de Fouchier reported a change in employment, but no conflict of interest was identified. Samuel Harvey participated in evidence reviews for key questions (4, 5, 6, 7, 13) and was found to have a significant conflict of interest. A conditional participation management plan was implemented, limiting his role to evidence review discussions without vocal or voting rights for recommendations 4, 5, 6, 7, and 13. Norito Kawakami declared research funds, paid consultancies, lecture honoraria, and an unpaid presidency of the Japan Society for Occupational Health, but no conflict of interest was identified. 5. Other GDG members, such as Anthony D., Neil Greenberg, Birgit Greiner, Nadine Harker, João Silvestre Silva-Junior, Angela Martin, Christina Maslach, Nina Hedegaard Nielsen, Reiner Rugulies, and Dieter Zapf, declared various professional roles, research funds, or consultancies, but no conflicts of interest were identified. 6. Evidence and supporting evidence team members, including Taylor Braund, Mark Deady, Raymond Lam, Akihito Shimazu, and Jo Yarker, also declared employment, research funds, or consultancies. No conflicts of interest were identified for these individuals. 7. Prior to the guideline development, an initial meeting called the Landscape Forum on Workplace Mental Health was held in Geneva, Switzerland, in November 2019. The primary objective was to discuss the extent of evidence for interventions addressing mental health in the workplace. Following this meeting, the WHO Steering Group conducted preliminary scoping of available evidence to prepare a draft scope for the guidelines. 8. The scope of the guidelines was reviewed and finalized during the first virtual meeting of the GDG in April 2020. This included discussions and agreements on the final scope and PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome) questions. Background questions were also developed to identify the best available evidence sources and provide contextual information for the guidelines. 9. The GDG, in consultation with the WHO Steering Group and the guideline methodologist, developed a list of outcomes relevant to specific PICO questions. Each outcome was rated on a scale from 1 to 9, with ratings indicating whether the outcome was critical (7–9), important (4–6), or not important (1–3) for decision-making. 10. Key questions addressed in the guidelines include: Universal organizational interventions to improve positive mental health and reduce symptoms of mental health conditions, suicidal behaviors, and substance use. Organizational interventions for specific worker groups, such as civilian health workers, emergency workers, and humanitarian workers, to improve mental health outcomes. Interventions for workers with symptoms of emotional distress or mental health conditions to improve mental health and reduce adverse outcomes. Training for managers to improve their knowledge, attitudes, and skills to support workers' mental health and well-being. Training for workers to enhance their knowledge and skills to support colleagues' mental health and well-being. Individual interventions, including psychosocial, physical activity, and health promotion interventions, to improve mental health outcomes. 11. Critical outcomes for these questions include mental health symptoms and disorders, positive mental health, quality of life, functioning, work-related outcomes, substance use, and suicidal behaviors. Important outcomes include adverse effects and satisfaction with care. 12. The guidelines also address interventions for individuals on leave due to mental health conditions, focusing on improving return-to-work rates, reducing absence, and enhancing mental health outcomes. 13. Screening programs for mental health conditions in the workplace are evaluated for their acceptability and effectiveness in reducing symptoms of mental health conditions among workers. Critical outcomes include mental health symptoms, user satisfaction, and work-related outcomes, while important outcomes include quality of life and adverse effects.
